feedback: If a learner compares 1/4 and 0.3 by surface digits, have them convert both to decimals (1/4 = 0.25) or to positions on the line; 0.25 sits below 0.3.
If a marker is pushed past the certain end, re-anchor: nothing is more likely than certain, so probability tops out at 1 — unlike a general fraction of a quantity, a probability cannot exceed 1.
If a probability is stated as a whole-number count of outcomes, point back to the line: a probability is a position between 0 and 1, not a tally.
activities.intendedInsight: A probability is one point on a bounded measure line; the same value can be written as a fraction, decimal or percentage, and nothing can lie below 0 or above 1.
learnerActions: Work with a 0-to-1 line marked with the fixed landmarks 0 (impossible), 1/2 (even chance) and 1 (certain).
Place a probability of 0.7 and a probability of 1/4 at their correct positions, and read off the same point shown three ways as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
For each placement, state which landmark the event sits near and justify its position ('0.7 is above even chance, so toward the certain end').
Place a set of everyday-event cards on the scale and justify each position in words.
Test the bounds: try to place a marker beyond the certain end or below the impossible end and state why no probability can go there.
activities.title: Placing probabilities on the 0-to-1 measure line

feedback: If a learner assigns 1/3 to every colour on the biased spinner, point back to the stated 70% and the unequal sections: equal probabilities require equal sections, which this spinner does not have.

If a learner says the drawing-pin probability is 1/2 ('two ways to land'), note that the pin is not symmetric — two outcomes do not make them equally likely, and no value is stated, so it must be read off where repeated data settle.
Reinforce: P(not red) = 1 − P(red); the complement is found by subtracting from the certain bound, not by counting colours.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal probabilities require equal sections/outcomes. For a biased device symmetry no longer gives the value: if the bias is stated you use the given value (red = 0.7); where neither symmetry nor a stated value is available (a drawing pin), the probability can only be estimated from repeated data. The scale applies in every case.
learnerActions: Start with a fair 3-section spinner (equal sections) and calculate each colour's probability as favourable/total — here the three colours genuinely sit at equal thirds; similarly a fair six-sided die gives each number a probability of 1/6 by symmetry.
Switch to a biased spinner that is STATED to be designed so red comes up 70% of the time, with the red section much larger. Predict where the three colours sit on the line BEFORE checking.

Use the stated 70% to place red, and run or observe repeated spins to see that the three colours do not come out at equal thirds — red's observed proportion tends to sit near 0.7, above even chance and toward the certain end, while blue and yellow together share roughly the remaining 0.3 (they may be close to each other, since their split is not given); a finite run only approximates each value rather than landing on it exactly.

Place P(red) = 0.7 above even chance, toward the certain end, and work out P(not red) = P(blue or yellow) = 0.3 by subtracting from 1, placing it below even chance (blue and yellow share that 0.3, and the split between them is not given).
State in words why 'three colours' did not guarantee '1/3 each' — only equal sections would.
Then consider a plain drawing pin, whose point-up probability is neither given by symmetry nor stated: decide that it can only be estimated from data, and explain why there is no symmetry to use.
activities.title: Fair vs biased: when symmetry works and when it doesn't

feedback: If the set is ordered by visible digits, require conversion to decimals first; the surface digits mislead (1/4 looks like '4' but is 0.25).
For a 'probability = 6' or 'probability > 1' choice, re-anchor on the certain bound: a probability tops out at 1.
For the '1/3 each' claim, accept only answers that tie the equal split to equal sections, and reject it for a biased spinner.
activities.intendedInsight: Probabilities written in different notations must be converted to a common form before comparison; values cannot exceed 1 or be raw counts; '1/n each' holds only for genuinely equal sections/outcomes.
learnerActions: Order a mixed set such as 40%, 1/4 and 0.3 from least to most likely by first converting all to a common form.
Convert each probability to a decimal (or a position on the line) and check: 1/4 = 0.25, which sits below 0.3, which sits below 40% = 0.4.
Decide whether each of several statements is possible — e.g. 'a probability of 6' or 'a probability bigger than 1' — and justify using the bounds.
Judge a fair-vs-biased claim: 'there are three colours, so each has probability 1/3' — decide whether it is right and explain when it would and would not hold.
activities.title: Ordering and converting mixed-notation probabilities

feedback: Prompt for the structural reason (section size, bounds), not just a yes/no answer.
If the learner stalls, direct them to place the value on the line and read off whether it is possible.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why values cannot exceed 1 and why '1/n each' needs equal sections consolidates the two central KS3 ideas in the learner's own words.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as 'Could a probability be 2?' and justify the answer using the 0–1 bounds.
Respond to 'Why isn't each colour 1/3 on this biased spinner?' and explain what would have to be true for 1/3 each to hold.
Explain how you would find P(not red) from P(red), and where it sits relative to even chance.
activities.title: Socratic challenges to the bounds and the 1/n shortcut
